awd_titl_txt: Conference: Workshop on the role of humanities in addressing ecological challenges
awd_abstract_narration:
This is a workshop organized by The National Humanities Alliance Foundation and the American Council of Learned Societies (ACLS) for approximately 25 attendees that brings together humanities scholars, their collaborators from STEM fields, and policymakers and funders to discuss the role of the humanities in multi-disciplinary projects that address ecological challenges. The workshop focuses on a broad range of projects that depend on the collaboration between the humanities and STEM fields. The aims include collecting information on types of projects, networks, funders, publication outlets, and policy impacts and to develop best practices for cultivating and sustaining these types of projects. A white paper will be produced and broadly disseminated. This project benefits societal welfare by helping to expand discussion and investigation of important current scientific issues to include the perspectives of humanities scholars.

The workshop is a one-day in-person workshop, following an open Call for Proposals. Workshop participants will come from a variety of identities and backgrounds, project types, disciplines, methodologies, career statuses, and experiences. The workshop day includes lightning talks, whole-group discussion, and small-group discussions. A post-workshop survey will evaluate the experiences of participants and value of the workshop. A white paper will be disseminated widely through various networks.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project examined how equal partnerships between humanities and STEM researchers can strengthen efforts to address ecological challenges and identified challenges to undertaking interdisciplinary work. The National Humanities Alliance and the American Council of Learned Societies sought to identify what these collaborations look like, what they contribute to research, and how universities and funders can better support them.

The project began with a national survey of humanities-STEM collaborations focused on environmental issues. Thirty-five respondents described projects, research methods, institutional partnerships, funding sources, public-engagement activities, and the roles played by different disciplines. The project team used these responses, together with additional research, to create a landscape map of the field. The map identified research centers, professional networks, funders, publication venues, policy-facing initiatives, and recurring forms of collaboration.

On January 23, 2026, the project convened researchers and funders in Washington, D.C. Participants represented projects involving sustainable agriculture, wildlife history, industrial pollution, mosquito-borne disease, brownfield mapping, river restoration, and the history of fire in Maine. The meeting enabled participants from different disciplines, institutions, career stages, and regions to compare approaches and identify common opportunities and obstacles.

The project's principal intellectual finding was that humanities and STEM methods produce stronger research when they shape projects together from the beginning. Humanities approaches contributed historical context, ethical analysis, oral history, storytelling, interpretation, and attention to how communities understand place, identity, risk, and responsibility. Scientific and technical approaches contributed measurement, modeling, mapping, computational tools, and hypothesis testing. Rather than treating the humanities merely as a means of communicating scientific results, researchers and community partners jointly developed research questions, evidence, and outcomes. Moreover, because these projects were strengthened by community partnerships, they tended to be grounded in concrete needs and had real-world impacts. 

The project also identified major barriers to this work. Building trust across disciplines and with communities often requires years, while grants commonly operate on short timelines and emphasize fixed deliverables. Participants reported difficulties compensating community partners, moving funds across departments, supporting staff, sustaining interdisciplinary centers, and receiving appropriate recognition through tenure and promotion systems.

A resulting white paper translated these findings into recommendations for funders and universities. These included longer and more flexible grants, support for exploratory relationship-building, direct funding pathways for community collaborators, sustained investment in interdisciplinary centers and staff, and greater recognition of collaborative and public-facing work.

The project's broader impacts include creating a new community of practice, connecting researchers with funders, and offering practical guidance for institutions seeking to support interdisciplinary research. By strengthening collaboration among scholars, communities, and decision-makers, the project demonstrated how humanities-STEM partnerships can produce more accurate, publicly relevant research and help communities turn knowledge into action.
